title: Additional no-op cases for <label>'s activation behavior
body:
[`label`](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/forms.html#the-label-element) elements have an activation behavior that allows the implementation to click on the labeled control, if it is customary for the platform the user agent runs on to do so. However, there is an explicit no-op clause "for events targeted at _interactive content_ descendants of a label element, and any descendants of those _interactive content_ descendants".

The purpose of this no-op clause is for cases like
```html
<label>
  <button>Labeled control</button>
  <button>Another button</button>
</label>
```
If the user clicks on the second button, the first should not automatically get clicked on also. Even more importantly, if the user clicks on the _first_ button, the browser should not implicitly click on it again, which would lead to an infinite recursion.

Modulo #5414, this all makes sense and is implemented. However, this no-op clause deals with _interactive content_ rather than _labelable elements_, which begs the question of what happens with non-interactive, but labelable, content. Consider instead
```html
<label>
  <progress onclick="console.log('first clicked')">Labeled control</progress>
  <progress onclick="console.log('second clicked')">Another progress</progress>
</label>
```
It appears that we want to have a similar guarantee here: clicking on the either `progress` element should not cause infinite recursion. But the spec doesn't say anything about this currently, and here's where implementations diverge. In Chrome and the WebKit-based GNOME Web (aka Epiphany), clicking on the first only prints "first clicked" once, while in Firefox the same line is printed twice. On the other hand, implementations agree that clicking the second progress should result in `second clicked` followed by one `first clicked`.

To implement Chrome's behavior, the following rule could be [used](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/master:third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/forms/html_label_element.cc;l=149-151;drc=5094a235259d7169c4c5acf4b636c640b5a05617):

> If the labeled control is a shadow-including inclusive ancestor of the event's target, then do nothing in `label`'s activation behavior. The labeled control has presumably already received this event.

To implement Firefox's behavior, the following rule could be [used](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/3a9dbc403f33cca1ff43326d78340add7d996350/dom/html/HTMLLabelElement.cpp#75-76):

> Any click event that ends up triggering the activation behavior of a `label` can only be forwarded by `label` once.

---

Two questions for us:

1. Do we want to standardize further on clicking some non-interactive but still labelable descendant of `label` elements?

   I believe the answer here is yes. We should prevent clearly problematic cases that may lead to infinite recursion, especially when implementations have converged on this point on their own. (See clicking on the second `progress` element.)

2. Which behavior do we want to standardize? Chrome/WebKit's or Firefox's?

   I think the Chrome/WebKit behavior makes more sense. I can't see what could be gained by having two click events rather than one on the same element.
